newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU electricity liberalisation faces parliamentary delay.
newsitem.headline: EU electricity liberalisation faces parliamentary delay.

text.p: The European Parliament will ask for extra time to prepare its view on the hard-fought compromise deal on electricity market liberalisation reached by EU energy ministers in June, raising the prospect of further delays.

Parliament officials said on Wednesday that the assembly was likely to ask for changes in the draft directive on creating an internal market in electricity, only agreed by EU member states after seven years of wrangling.
The sensitive dossier may even need to go to conciliation between the Parliament and the Council, they said.
This may put the January 1 date for the directive's entry into force in jeopardy.
"There will be some amendments. The question is: do we have just some technical amendments or do we have some which are really political," one Parliament official said.

The Parliament's Committee on Research, Technological Development and Energy will ask the Council for a one-month extension of the three-month period within which Parliament must deliver its opinion at its second reading of the dossier.

If the request is accepted, the new deadline for the Parliament's opinion would be January 6. This could dash hopes that EU energy ministers would be able to formally adopt the directive at their December 3 meeting.

Stressing the importance of the dossier, another Parliament official said the assembly had the right to request an extension in order to avoid difficulties. The directive falls under the co-decision procedure which gives Parliament much say over it.

"It (the electricity directive) is a delicate matter," the official said, adding that the dossier would probably need to go to conciliation between the Council and the Parliament, which could last for up to six weeks.

While no clear-cut opposition to the proposed new rules on creating an internal electricity market was expected by Parliament, the official said he believed the assembly would adopt amendments, which the Council may not accept.
"I don't think there is any kind of declared intention of rejecting it," he said, but added: "I don't think Parliament would abstain from coming up with some amendments, even of a technical nature."
In a Parliament statement issued on Tuesday, parliament rapporteur Claude Desama said it was necessary to "proceed with caution and not confuse speed with haste."

"The European Parliament will need to build a broad consensus to underpin the amendments for second reading. With that end in view, the rapporteur will be embarking on a round of talks with the political groups next week," the statement said.
Neither the Irish presidency not the Commission had yet heard about the energy committee's request.

Both an Irish official and a Commission official said they had received the indication from Parliament that the dossier would come up at the November session, enabling it to be adopted at the Energy Council in December. If it instead goes to the December session and if there are no problems it may be adopted without discussion as an "A-point" at any other Council.

The deal reached by EU energy ministers at a special session last June was a hard-fought compromise between countries such as Germany and Britain, which were pushing for far-reaching liberalisation, and France, wary of any dramatic such moves.
It will allow mainly large industrial firms to freely shop around for the best deal.
Under the compromise deal, nearly a quarter of the EU's overall market for electricity would be open to competition from January 1999. This would rise to nearly a third by 2003.
It also went some way towards taking on board the concerns of the Parliament, if not all of them.

Speaking at the European Parliament in July, Irish Energy Minister Michael Lowry stressed that the deal was the result of a difficult compromise. "I would ask Parliament to bear the difficulty and time consuming nature of these efforts in mind when considering the draft directive," he said.
